original_question: For each integer k > 2, does the Diophantine equation y = 2 x1 x2 ... xk + 1 have infinitely many solutions in prime numbers?
target_in_paper: Unsolved Problem 11 (Conjecture): for each positive integer k > 2, the paper asks whether the Diophantine equation y = 2 x1 x2 ... xk + 1 has infinitely many solutions in which all variables are prime. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's exact target: it has the right equation, the right quantifier on k, and the right infinitude question for prime solutions. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
missing_details: State explicitly that k is a fixed positive integer with k > 2, and the infinitude question is asked separately for each such k. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

Specify the full variable set and domain: x1, x2, ..., xk, and y are all required to be prime numbers, so the problem is over the integers with every variable restricted to primes. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

Clarify that the conjecture asks for infinitely many prime solution tuples (x1, ..., xk, y), not merely one prime value of y arising from some prime inputs. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

Do not add extra hypotheses not stated in the paper: no pairwise distinctness, ordering, parity restriction, or size condition on the primes is imposed. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

No additional structural conditions such as homogeneity, degree bounds, field assumptions, or nilpotency appear here; this is simply an arithmetic conjecture about prime solutions to one explicit Diophantine equation. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
refined_question: For each fixed positive integer k > 2, are there infinitely many tuples of prime numbers (x1, x2, ..., xk, y) such that y = 2 x1 x2 ... xk + 1, with no further assumptions such as distinctness or ordering of the primes? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
justification: The draft matches Unsolved Problem 11 almost exactly. The only refinements needed to make it fully stand-alone and maximally faithful are to say that k is fixed first, to name all variables, and to make explicit that every variable is prime. The same page supplies only illustrative examples, such as 571 = 2·3·5·19 + 1 and 647 = 2·17·19 + 1, and does not give an equivalent reformulation or any extra hidden hypotheses. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
